content.passage: Science and technology work together to make changes to our lives. Our scientific knowledge makes it possible for us to create and build new technologies. Then, these technologies often help us to discover new things about our world. And this can add to our existing scientific knowledge, which might then mean we create a new technology, and so it continues. If we don't have a certain technology, then we may not be able to develop in science. Let's look at an example. In the 1800s, a new technology was invented called the cathode-ray tube. By passing electricity through a glass tube, scientists were able to see something called electrons. Without the cathode-ray tube, we wouldn't have TVs, computers or phone screens today. In 1895, scientist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed that his cathode-ray tube was producing other rays that passed through paper, some metals and skin, but not through bone. With this scientific knowledge, scientists invented the X-ray machine, which we now use in hospitals all over the world. In 1914, father and son, William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg, used this technology to pass X-rays through crystals, so that they could see the atoms in the crystal. It was this scientific knowledge that allowed Rosalind Franklin to discover the shape of DNA in 1952.

content.script: Hello and welcome to the lecture. So, social media really started in 2003 with LinkedIn and was followed one year later by Facebook. We share information about ourselves online all the time by researching and buying things, and companies use that information to connect with us and sell us products. This will continue, and social media will be used more and more by companies to get information about us. Nowadays, most social media sites cover a wide range of topics, but in the future we're likely to see an increase in more specific sites.
